comments.author: WubsGames

sorta!

The best AI tool i've found so far is Gemini, it will happily make little web games, and even some windows games.

But there isn't currently a model that will produce full production level 3d games.  
We will have to wait a little while longer for that.

We are probably entering an era where gamedev will be most accessible, but we are only just starting to enter that era.

Also keep in mind that running these AI models is expensive, Was able to rack up a $70 Gemini bill pretty quickly, working on even a simple demo project. Having Gemini build something like Counterstrike would probably still cost as much as just hiring some cheap developers to build it.

EDIT:

Meshy is a great tool for making 3d models from images, their new low-poly version is actually almost useable for games. You could get away with just chucking some Meshy models into a simple looking 3d game right now.

comments.author: erofamiliar
comments.body:
Oh no, lmao. Go try it \*right now\*. I guarantee that, no, you yourself will absolutely need to learn unreal engine and how to make characters and how to make characters react to open doors. AI constantly fucks up if you don't explain to it how you want things done, it gets VERY expensive if you want the AI to actually have all of your code in context at once, and it needs to have that context if you want it to give you something that's actually useful.

I have found it extremely helpful when I'm not raging at it, though! But if the AI is in control, it'll make dipshit decisions over and over and over, constantly kneecapping itself to achieve whatever the most immediate goal is with zero regard for the integrity of the project itself, all while making the most ridiculous assumptions and asking you the equivalent of "is the monitor plugged in? the keyboard? the problem might be between the monitor and the chair?" whenever the code that it wrote doesn't quite work the way it says it should. You don't need to know how to write your code, but you need to understand how it works, or you won't understand when it doesn't work.

...Or maybe that's all just ChatGPT, I don't know. Gemini does it too but it's not quite as bad about it.

replies.author: erofamiliar
replies.body:
dog 😭 I'm telling you, you need to understand what the script is doing. It isn't about just "script rotates door to open it". You need to know

* does the door push people?
* does the door push specifically the player?
* does the door push physics objects?
* is it stopped from closing by physics objects?
* can the player open the door at any time?
   * if not, when can they open the door?
   * if not, when can't they?
* can enemies open the door?
   * if not, when can they open the door?
   * if not, when can't they open the door?
* what if the door has a lock?

and so on... It isn't about making scripts in isolation, *anyone* can make a script in isolation. The problem is you want to make a videogame. This isn't gatekeeping, I'm not saying you can't do it, but I am saying it is a very bad idea to ship a reasonably complex game solo without understanding how it functions, even moreso if you're using today's AI to code it. You're probably all set if you're making flappy bird with doors, though.

I'm not telling you that you need to write all of the boilerplate code yourself. I'm telling that you need to understand it, even if you aren't writing it. If you don't, the moment your game becomes more than a few hundred lines of code and something breaks, you will pull your hair out in frustration trying to fix it.

I would love to see the trailer when you've got one.

replies.author: Punished_Nuts
replies.body:
> but I am saying it is a very bad idea to ship a reasonably complex game solo without understanding how it functions, even moreso if you're using today's AI to code it

Shipping a game without understanding how it works will always be a horrible idea, because you will fuck up and you will need to patch out your mistakes no matter how good of a dev you are, and not knowing how your project works makes this exponentially harder. This is the sort of thing that will always be true, regardless of what method you are using in creating a game.

replies.author: erofamiliar
replies.body:
Yep! I'm just hedging my language because the moment you start talking in absolutes, some guy comes out of the woodwork to go "Well actually-". It's just a matter of time before AI does something funky in your code, and if you don't know what it's doing, the AI will give you a hundred different ways to fix it and none of them will be correct. 
And to be clear, I use AI code and like AI code, but it has to exist alongside engine and dev knowledge, it can't replace it.

comments.author: jon11888
comments.body:
I feel like there are two kinds of people using AI to make games. Low effort cash grab asset flippers, and people with a genuine interest in AI as a creative tool. Maybe a bit of overlap when both apply.


I haven't seen very many games that openly use AI extensively, but I'm curious to see how things develop.


I'm optimistic that we'll see some fascinating games made by people with a genuine passion for AI.


I'm also dreading the waves of soulless churned out slop of a similar kind to what we saw back when low budget unity asset flips first started showing up on steam and kickstarter.
